imageCaption: Anthony's pegboard of license plates catches morning light through the kitchen window—a patchwork map of everywhere they've been, with one blank space that refuses to stay empty.
text:
The morning after the potluck, Aaliyah woke up to the sound of her father swearing at license plates.

Not angry swearing. Confused swearing. The specific tone Anthony used when something he'd been certain about had decided to rearrange itself without asking permission.

She found him in the kitchen, his pegboard spread across the entire dining table. It was a stunning artifact—seventy-nine countries and territories, each with their own small replica plate hanging from careful hooks. A map made of traveled-to places. A visual record of a family that had decided spontaneity was a valid life philosophy.

Except one plate was different.

"It's blank," Anthony said. Not asking. Stating facts like a man who'd woken up at 6:47 AM to watch his own collection betray him. "I pinned it yesterday. I know I pinned it. The Barbados plate was right here—I got it from that vendor near the harbor, remember? The one who told me about her daughter's wedding?"

Aaliyah leaned closer. The space where the Barbados plate should have been was holding something else now—a plate that existed in a state of almost-but-not-quite. Like it was written in a language she could almost read. Like it was a place that hadn't decided to be real yet.

"Is this a glitch?" she asked.

"Worse," her father said. "It's a choice. My plates don't glitch. They don't change. They document what we did. But this one—" He pointed at the blank-not-blank plate. "This one is documenting what we're going to do."

Sully padded into the kitchen, took one look at the altered pegboard, and barked three times. Not alarm. Not warning. Acknowledgment.

Minor glitch nearby. Specifically, in the collection of miniature license plates.

"Okay," Aaliyah said, pulling up a chair. "Start from the beginning. What exactly did you notice?"

"I was going to reorganize them by continent," Anthony explained, which was so unlike him that Aaliyah felt her analytical mind stop and pay attention. Anthony didn't reorganize things. Anthony believed that chaotic arrangement was a narrative about the journey, not the geography. "Not today. Just... thinking ahead. Making a plan, which, I know, is weird for me. But after yesterday, I wanted to understand the route. I wanted to see if there was a pattern to where we've been."

He pointed at the board. "Look at the path. Lisbon to Tokyo to Nairobi to Buenos Aires to Reykjavik to—" He stopped. "To here. To home. And then the route just stops. There's no next plate."

"Because we haven't gone to the next place yet," Aaliyah said carefully.

"Right. Except—" He held up the blank plate. It seemed to shift between being a real object and being a suggestion of a future object. "—Except I went to get the Barbados plate this morning because I thought we might head that direction. The Caribbean seems like a natural progression. Warm weather, good food, Lulu's been looking at real estate in that region. And I pinned it. I was holding this board in one hand and I pinned the Barbados plate and I felt it catch properly. But when I looked down..."

"It was blank," Aaliyah finished.

"It was blank," he confirmed. "And not like it wasn't printed. Like it was printed and then something looked at it and decided it wasn't the right answer. Like the board was telling me: no, wrong direction."

Luisana appeared in the doorway with her hair still wet and her journal already in hand. She had the expression of someone who'd woken up knowing her family needed her. "Did Anthony's license plates just talk to us?"

"One of them did," Aaliyah said. "It's telling us we're not going to Barbados."

"Oh," Luisana said, sitting down. She opened her journal and started writing immediately. "That's interesting, because I had a dream about Curaçao. Very specific dream. The yellow house. The one I've been looking at listings for."

"We're not even close to that route," Anthony said. "That would mean—"

"That the board is showing us the actual next place," Aaliyah interrupted, understanding settling into her like a stone into water. "Not the logical next place. Not the safe next place. The actual next place the timeline needs us to go."

She looked at her father. "Can you take the plate out?"

"I tried. It won't come out. It's pinned but it's not, and whatever I try to grab just slides through it like it's made of something that isn't quite matter."

Sully jumped up on a chair—which broke three different household rules but nobody corrected him because he appeared to be trying to get a closer look at the impossible plate. He sniffed it. Then he sneezed. Then he looked at Anthony with the specific expression that meant: you're holding the map wrong.

"What if it's not telling you where not to go?" Aaliyah said slowly. "What if it's showing you the place that will only exist if you believe in it before you get there?"

She pulled out her phone and opened her glitch logs. Seventy-nine documented temporal anomalies. Seventy-nine moments where the timeline had bent because her family was moving through it with genuine joy and chaos.

"Look at the pattern," she said, pulling up her mapping notes. "Every glitch we've stabilized has moved us closer to something. Not farther away. We haven't stopped at any place twice. We've never gone backward. What if the board is showing you the final destination?"

"Curaçao," Luisana said softly. "The board is showing you Curaçao."

Anthony looked at the impossible plate. Then at his wife. Then at his daughter. Then at his dog, who nodded like Sully had been waiting for all of them to catch up.

"We're not ready to stop yet," Anthony said, but there was a question in it.

"No," Aaliyah agreed. "But the timeline knows where we're stopping. And it's being patient. It's just leaving us a compass."

The blank plate caught the morning light. For just a moment, it looked almost like a place. Like yellow buildings reflected in water. Like a harbor. Like home.

"Well," Luisana said, writing faster. "I suppose I should tell you both about the house with the blue door. The one I've been looking at. It's got a view of the water, and there's a snorkel shop two blocks away, and I think it might be where we're supposed to understand what the last hundred days were for."

Sully barked once, satisfied, and stole a piece of toast from the counter that nobody had left for stealing.

The pegboard sat on the table between them—seventy-nine known places and one place that wasn't real yet but absolutely would be.

All they had to do was move toward it.
